story.title: UN General Assembly Adopts New Map Reflecting Africa's True Size
story.summary: The UN General Assembly has voted to adopt a new world map that more accurately represents the size of continents, particularly Africa. The resolution, initiated by several African nations and co-sponsored by France, received support from 164 member states, with only the United States voting against it. The new map replaces the traditional Mercator projection, which has been criticized for distorting the sizes of countries and continents.

explore_lenses.label: What does the new map actually correct?
explore_lenses.title: Area accuracy, not a perfect map
explore_lenses.summary: Equal Earth preserves the relative areas of landmasses, addressing Mercator’s large area inflation near the poles. It is not a universally superior projection: every flat world map trades off some geographic properties.

claims.text: The International Cartographic Association says Equal Earth is appropriate when comparing geographic area, while Mercator preserves angles and is useful for navigation but strongly distorts area at world scale.

The UN resolution’s sponsors argued that Mercator-based maps affect education, public understanding and perceptions of Africa and other equatorial regions, framing the issue as one of equitable representation and “cognitive justice.”
Cartography experts caution that Equal Earth also distorts angles, distances and shapes, and that no single projection is correct for every purpose.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The resolution promotes Equal Earth for contexts where relative area matters; it does not establish it as the sole technically valid world-map projection.

explore_lenses.label: How did an African-led campaign reach the UN?
explore_lenses.title: From regional advocacy to a UN vote
explore_lenses.summary: The vote followed an African Union-backed effort led diplomatically by Togo and supported by advocacy groups. The campaign turned a longstanding cartographic debate into a formal General Assembly question about education and representation.

claims.text: The resolution was championed by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by a recorded vote of 164 in favor, one against and six abstentions on September 4, 2026.
The African Union said the initiative sought a representation of Africa based on objectively and scientifically established realities, rather than the relative areas displayed by Mercator.
Associated Press reported that the UN vote culminated a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups; the African Union had previously endorsed the broader Correct the Map initiative.

explore_lenses.label: Will schools and digital maps now change?
explore_lenses.title: A voluntary shift with practical limits
explore_lenses.summary: The resolution encourages wider use of equal-area maps but does not mandate replacement of Mercator. Implementation will depend on choices by governments, UN bodies, publishers, schools and technology platforms.

claims.text: The adopted text calls for wider use of equal-area projections, particularly Equal Earth, where comparative continental size is relevant; it does not ban Mercator or impose a compulsory replacement.

The African Union Commission said it will work with Togo, member states and relevant partners, and urged educational systems, publishers, international institutions and digital platforms to progressively use maps that better reflect land area.

The United States representative opposed the resolution as part of a broader ideological project, while Ukraine said it did not oppose the principle but objected to how the cited Equal Earth map depicts Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory; the EU said the measure should not affect sovereignty or borders.

story_report.summary: The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution promoting wider use of equal-area world maps, particularly the Equal Earth projection, in settings where comparisons of continental size matter. The measure, championed by Togo on behalf of the African Group, passed on Sept. 4, 2026, by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions; the United States cast the sole vote against. The resolution does not prohibit Mercator maps, but encourages an alternative intended to represent relative land area more accurately.

sections.heading: Equal Earth and Mercator Uses
sections.body: The Equal Earth design, introduced in 2018, is suited to comparing geographic area, according to the International Cartographic Association. Mercator preserves angles and remains useful for navigation, but it substantially distorts area on a world-scale map. Equal Earth also involves trade-offs, including distortions of angles, distances and shapes; cartography experts say no single projection is technically correct for every use.

sections.heading: African Campaign for Map Representation
sections.body: Sponsors argued that Mercator-based maps influence education, public understanding and perceptions of Africa and other equatorial regions, describing the issue as one of equitable representation and “cognitive justice.” The African Union said the initiative sought a depiction of Africa based on objectively and scientifically established realities rather than Mercator’s relative-area display. The vote followed a campaign involving African countries and advocacy groups, after the African Union endorsed the broader Correct the Map initiative.

sections.heading: Voting Objections and Territorial Concerns
sections.body: The U.S. representative characterized the resolution as part of a broader ideological project. Ukraine said it supported the principle but objected to the depiction of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory on the cited Equal Earth map, while the European Union said the measure should not affect sovereignty or borders. Public reporting does not provide a complete account of the negotiations or every country’s rationale for its vote.

unresolved.text: No binding compliance mechanism, implementation deadline or confirmed timetable has been announced for changes to school curricula, commercial mapping software or national maps.

related_stories.title: UK Responds to Argentina's Renewed Falklands Claims Amid Political Tensions
related_stories.summary: The UK government has reaffirmed its commitment to the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands following remarks from Argentina's President Javier Milei, who claimed that 'winds of change' are favoring Argentina's position on the islands. In response, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband emphasized the UK's unwavering support for the self-determination of the Falkland Islanders. This exchange comes amid heightened tensions, particularly with suggestions from Donald Trump that the US may reconsider its stance on the issue.

related_stories.title: King Oyo's Body Returns to Uganda for Burial Following His Death
related_stories.summary: The body of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, recognized as the world's youngest reigning monarch, has returned to Uganda for burial. The king passed away in the United States at the age of 34 after battling an aggressive form of cancer.

related_stories.title: U.S. Military Destroys Three Iranian Oil Tankers Following Attacks
related_stories.summary: The U.S. military reported that it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers, including the M/T Downy and M/T Stark 1, after Iran launched ballistic missile attacks targeting U.S. naval vessels. The U.S. Central Command stated that the attacks on the tankers were a response to Iran's failed missile strikes against a U.S. aircraft carrier and a destroyer.

related_stories.title: Mistrial Declared in Lindsay Clancy's Murder Case After Jury Deadlock
related_stories.summary: A mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial after the jury was unable to reach a unanimous decision following seven days of deliberation. The trial lasted over five weeks and included extensive testimony. Clancy's defense attorney criticized a juror for allegedly obstructing an acquittal. Patrick Clancy expressed that facing another trial would be extremely painful for the family.
